argument against miracles is this: with respect to any alleged miracle, the extent to which evidence can show that scepticism relating to the historical question is unjustified will necessarily constitute the very same evidence for showing that scepticism relating to the conceptual question is justified. Conversely, any evidence which showed that it would be unreasonable to be sceptical concerning the conceptual question would constitute the very same evidence for justifying scepticism concerning the historicity of the alleged event.

To unpack this, we must first distinguish between two distinct types of skepticism that Hume’s argument targets. The **historical question** asks: "Did this event actually happen?" The **conceptual question** asks: "Is it logically coherent to classify this event as a 'miracle'?" Hume’s dilemma posits a zero-sum game between these two inquiries. If you present strong evidence that an event *did* happen (thereby defeating historical skepticism), that very same evidence simultaneously proves that the event was *not* a miracle (thereby justifying conceptual skepticism). Why? Because, in Hume’s framework, the definition of a miracle is inextricably linked to the violation of natural law. If the evidence is strong enough to confirm the event occurred, it is strong enough to show that the natural law was *not* violated (perhaps the cause was unknown but natural). Therefore, the more you prove the event happened, the less you can claim it was a supernatural miracle. Conversely, if you have evidence that the event *was* a true supernatural miracle (defeating conceptual skepticism), that same evidence implies the event could not have happened in the natural world, thus justifying skepticism about its historicity.

One obvious way to refute the Humean dilemma is to provide at least one counter-example in the form of a description of some logically possible event, set in logically possible circumstances of a particular kind, such that if an event answering to this description were to occur in such circumstances, it would be unreasonable for anyone to deny that a miracle had actually taken place. Whether there has in fact been an event and set of circumstances satisfying those conditions would of course be a separate question, but all we need in order to destroy the a priori argument is just one logically possible, hypothetical, counter-example. Then the question whether any miracles have in fact occurred, or might occur in the future, would at least be an open one, and (at least in principle) an answerable one.

Here, the strategy shifts from defending specific miracles to attacking the logical structure of Hume’s argument itself. To dismantle an *a priori* argument (an argument based on logic and definitions rather than empirical observation), you do not need to prove that miracles have happened. You only need to demonstrate that it is **logically possible** for them to happen. Think of it like a legal defense: you don’t need to prove your client is innocent; you only need to show that the law, as interpreted by the prosecution, is flawed or that a scenario exists where the accusation doesn't hold. If we can construct a hypothetical scenario where an event occurs and it is *unreasonable* to deny it was a miracle, we break Hume’s dilemma. We show that historical evidence and conceptual justification can coexist. This does not prove miracles exist; it merely proves that the question "Do miracles exist?" is not logically closed off. It remains an open, answerable question based on evidence, rather than a logical impossibility.

In order to refute Hume, it is not sufficient simply to point out that it is surely logically possible that water should turn into wine, or a rod turn into a serpent, or a dead man rise from the dead. Incredibly, some have taken Hume to be denying this, and have taken him to task for so conveniently foregetting his own philosophical principles. After all it was Hume himself who insisted that
the mind can always conceive ... any event to follow upon another; whatever we conceive is possible, at least in a metaphysical sense. $^{2}$

A common pitfall for critics of Hume is to misunderstand the scope of his claim. Many assume Hume is arguing that miracles are *logically impossible*—that is, that they violate the laws of logic or metaphysics. This is a misreading. Hume was a thoroughgoing empiricist and a proponent of logical possibility. As he explicitly stated, the human mind can conceive of any sequence of events, and whatever we can conceive is, at least in a metaphysical sense, possible. Therefore,

Hume would certainly not deny that it is logically possible for a dead man to rise from the dead. Nor would he deny that, when expressed in general terms, the notion of a dead man rising from the dead is a notion of a truly miraculous event. What he would deny is that it is logically possible for anyone to have good reason simultaneously to believe both that such an event had in fact taken place, and that that particular event was indeed a miracle. Exactly why he would deny this is not all that obvious. Still less obvious is whether he is justified in denying it. But that he does deny it, and that the basis of his denial is what he takes to be the particular logical relations which hold between the concepts of miracle and evidence (or good reason) I propose to assume without argument. My main concern is to see whether the denial can be justified.

This distinction is crucial. Hume is not saying "A dead man cannot rise." He is saying "You cannot have *good reason* to believe a dead man rose *and* that it was a miracle." He is attacking the epistemology (the theory of knowledge) of miracle claims, not the metaphysics of resurrection. He argues that the concepts of "miracle" and "evidence" are logically entangled in such a way that strong evidence for the event destroys the claim that it is a miracle. The author of this text accepts, for the sake of argument, that Hume holds this view and that it is based on the logical relationship between these concepts. The author’s task is not to debate whether Hume *should* hold this view, but to investigate whether the view itself is logically defensible.

While this reply is adequate as far as it goes, it leaves untouched the much more formidable problem of whether we could ever have reason to believe that a truly anomalous event had occurred, even if it is granted that such events are logically possible. For it would seem that there is no way that we can have reason to believe that some particular event has taken place except by making use of inductive evidence. That is to say, any claim that we have evidence that an anomalous event has occurred, would itself necessarily depend on the tacit assumption that events in the natural world in some sense constitute a vast network of exceptionless regularities. Therefore, because nothing could count as evidence for an event's occurrence without our making assumptions not only concerning what has happened in the past but also about what must happen, as well as what cannot possibly happen, it would seem that to claim that we have evidence that what cannot possibly happen nevertheless has happened would involve us in a manifest contradiction.

It is this argument which constitutes the essence of the Humean argument against miracles and the first to see this clearly was Antony Flew. $^{4}$ The latest follower of this line of interpretation is P. S. Wadia who puts the point in this way:

No one can be justified in both thinking that it is reasonable to accept beliefs arrived at inductively and thinking, at the same time, that it may sometimes be reasonable to believe in the occurrence of a miracle.
He argues that those who claim that

it is not unreasonable to believe that ‘on occasion the physically impossible occurs’ cannot do so without at some point in their argument being forced to appeal to the very conception of rationality that they must begin by rejecting. $^{5}$

Unfortunately, Wadia himself confuses the issue when at another point he insists that 'it is certainly logically possible for someone to be in a position reasonably to conclude that the balance of evidence proves that a law of nature has been violated. I now want to argue that, Hume's argument to the contrary notwithstanding, not only does it make sense to suppose that we could have grounds for thinking that a physically impossible event had occurred but that we could even have grounds for thinking that an anomalous event had occurred, i.e. an event which would remain permanently inexplicable in naturalistic or scientific terms. $^{8}$

unpack this claim, we must first clarify the distinction between what is merely *unlikely* and what is *physically impossible*. In the context of this argument, a "physically impossible" event is one that violates the fundamental laws of nature as we currently understand them—laws that are not just strong tendencies, but absolute constraints. An "anomalous" event, as defined here, is a specific type of impossibility: it is an occurrence that defies all naturalistic or scientific explanation permanently. It is not just a gap in our current knowledge that might be filled by a future discovery; it is a permanent break in the causal chain of the physical world.

In order to show this, let us imagine that you, the reader, along with a handful of other witnesses, are present in my study as I write this paper. You know that, in the course of writing it, the pencil I am using will not turn into a lizard, since such an event is physically impossible. But suppose two minutes from now it nevertheless happened.

pause to analyze the logic of this scenario. We are establishing a baseline of certainty. Based on our understanding of physics, biology, and material science, we are justified in predicting that a graphite-and-wood object cannot spontaneously reorganize into a living reptile. This prediction is not a guess; it is a deduction from the laws of conservation of mass, energy, and biological complexity.
Of course, even if you think you saw it happen you would be right (i.e. justified) not to believe it, for after all, we have all seen rabbits being pulled out of empty hats.

the argument anticipates the most common objection: human perception is fallible. The "rabbit in the hat" analogy serves as a powerful reminder that our senses can be deceived by magic tricks, optical illusions, or simple errors in observation. Therefore, the immediate, raw experience of seeing the transformation is not, by itself, sufficient evidence. A rational observer would initially default to the explanation that is most probable: "I must be mistaken, or I am being tricked."

Nevertheless, we can easily imagine that we could satisfy ourselves that it was not an illusion or a clever conjuring trick provided we had full opportunity beforehand to check out the pencil as well as the room, condition of the observers, etc., and (after the event) the lizard.

is the crucial pivot in the argument. The author is not asking us to accept the event on faith; rather, they are asking us to consider a scenario where we have rigorously eliminated all mundane explanations. Imagine we had spent hours inspecting the pencil for hidden compartments. We had scanned the room for hidden doors or mirrors. We had verified that the witnesses were sober, sane, and not conspiring to deceive one another. And after the event, we could examine the lizard, confirming it was a genuine, living animal, not a prop.

Though such checks might need to be very elaborate, it seems hard to maintain that no matter how thorough and meticulous they were it would always be more reasonable to conclude that the pencil had not turned into a lizard after all.

sentence challenges the idea that skepticism is an infinite regress. If we have done everything a rational person *can* do to verify the facts, is it still rational to deny the event? The argument suggests that at some point, the weight of the evidence shifts. If every possible alternative explanation (trickery, hallucination, error) has been systematically ruled out, the remaining hypothesis—that the impossible actually happened—becomes the most reasonable conclusion, even if it contradicts our prior expectations.

Admittedly, we might be in some legitimate doubt as to whether that was the correct way of describing the event. But even if we preferred to say that at a particular moment the pencil ceased to exist and at precisely that same moment a lizard came into existence in its place, we would still be faced with a physically impossible event having happened.

the author addresses a potential semantic loophole. One might argue, "Well, maybe the pencil didn't *turn into* a lizard; maybe it just vanished and a lizard appeared." This is a subtle but important distinction. Does the *mechanism* of the change matter? The author argues that it does not. Whether we describe the event as a transformation (A becomes B) or a substitution (A disappears, B appears), the underlying physical reality is the same: the continuity of the physical world has been broken. The conservation of matter and energy has been violated. Therefore, the event remains physically impossible regardless of the specific linguistic description we choose.

And this would mean that we were wrong in predicting that it would not happen. Furthermore, though we claimed we knew it would not happen, if it did then obviously we could not have known that it would not.

section tackles the epistemological status of our knowledge. If the event occurs, our prior prediction ("The pencil will not turn into a lizard") was false. In philosophy, "knowledge" is often defined as justified true belief. If the belief turns out to be false, we did not have knowledge, even if we were justified in holding that belief. This is a key insight: being *justified* in a belief is different from the belief being *true*. We can be perfectly rational and still be wrong if the universe behaves in a way we didn't anticipate.

But this does not mean that we were not justified in claiming that we knew that it would not, for the simple reason that this knowledge-claim is about as well grounded as any empirical knowledge-claim can possibly be.

is the core of the defense against Hume. The author argues that our confidence in the laws of nature is not absolute certainty, but it is the *highest possible degree of justification* available to empirical science. We are not claiming to have divine insight into the future; we are claiming that, based on all available evidence, the probability of the event is effectively zero. If we are not justified in making this claim, then we are not justified in making *any* scientific claim.
If we are not justified in claiming to know that pencils cannot turn into lizards then we are not justified in claiming to know anything.

is a reductio ad absurdum argument. If we accept that we cannot be justified in believing that physically impossible events won't happen, we must also reject our confidence in gravity, thermodynamics, and biology. We would be left in a state of radical skepticism where no empirical prediction is valid. Since we are not in such a state (we do trust that the sun will rise and that objects fall when dropped), we must accept that we *are* justified in believing that physically impossible events will not occur. This justification is strong enough to serve as a baseline for rational belief, even if it is theoretically possible for that baseline to be overturned by an anomalous event.

pause here to unpack the logical architecture of this claim. The author is addressing a potential counter-argument: "If the impossible actually happens, doesn't that prove we were wrong to think it was impossible?" The author argues "no." The distinction lies between *epistemic justification* (our right to believe something based on current evidence) and *ontological status* (the actual nature of the event). Even if a miracle occurs, it doesn't necessarily mean our prior scientific models were "wrong" in a way that invalidates the concept of anomaly. It simply means the event falls outside the scope of natural law.

I grant that it is not so easy to see how we could be justified in regarding an event as being permanently inexplicable in naturalistic or scientific terms. For on the face of it, if an event has actually occurred, and we know that it has, then we would expect some sort of explanation as to why it had occurred to be in the offing.

the author acknowledges a significant hurdle for the reader. In the scientific mindset, "occurrence" implies "explainability." If you see a pencil turn into a lizard, your immediate instinct is to look for the mechanism: Was it a chemical reaction? A hologram? A sleight of hand? The phrase "in the offing" suggests that an explanation is imminent, waiting to be discovered. This is the default assumption of naturalism: every event has a natural cause.

But could we have grounds for concluding that no matter how much evidence we were to gather, and no matter what should turn out to be the future evolution of science, a scientific explanation would never be forthcoming?

is the critical question. It asks if there is a limit to scientific inquiry. Can we ever be *certain* that a natural explanation is impossible, or are we always left with the possibility that "we just haven't figured it out yet"? The author is setting up a scenario to test whether we can ever cross the threshold from "unexplained" to "supernatural."
Perhaps not, if this pencil turned into a lizard simply in the course of my writing this paper.

this baseline scenario: You are reading this, and suddenly, a pencil on your desk transforms into a live lizard. In this isolated context, the most rational conclusion is *not* that a god intervened. Instead, you would suspect:
1.  **Fraud:** A hidden mechanism or a trick of the light.
2.  **Illusion:** A hallucination or a sophisticated hologram.
3.  **Unknown Physics:** A bizarre, previously undiscovered natural law.

Because the context is mundane (just writing a paper), the burden of proof for a supernatural explanation is insurmountably high. The "simplest explanation" (Occam's Razor) would almost certainly point to a human trick or a natural anomaly.

But I think we can conceive of circumstances such that we would be justified not only in concluding that a physically impossible event had indeed taken place, but also that that event was rightly to be regarded as anomalous in the defined sense.

author is now proposing a shift in context. The key variable here is not the *event* itself (pencil to lizard), but the *context* in which it occurs. By changing the setting, we change the probability distribution of possible causes.

For let us now suppose that the turning of the pencil into a lizard occurred in a context more recognizably religious than the present context. Let us suppose that some popularly acclaimed holy-man or prophet declared that he was a chosen prophet of Mazda the god of light, and that he would call upon his god to show his power by turning a pencil into a lizard.

are now moving from a random occurrence to a *predicted* occurrence within a specific theological framework. The introduction of "Mazda the god of light" (a deity from Zoroastrianism) provides a specific causal agent. The prophet’s declaration acts as a hypothesis: "If I am the true prophet of Mazda, then Mazda will perform this specific miracle."

We would again need to check with meticulous thoroughness that all possibility of fraud and trickery was ruled out, but provided that there were no limitations at all placed on our checking investigations, both before and after the event, there seems no reason to suppose that we could not be rationally satisfied on that point.

is a crucial methodological safeguard. The author does not ask us to suspend our critical faculties. Instead, they demand *hyper-rigorous* scrutiny. We must assume the role of the most skeptical investigator possible. We check for wires, cameras, chemical residues, and psychological manipulation. The condition "no limitations at all placed on our checking investigations" is vital. It means we have the time, resources, and freedom to verify every detail. If, after this exhaustive process, we find no trace of fraud, the "natural explanation" hypothesis begins to collapse.

Let us further suppose that not only did our holy man succeed in bringing it about that a pencil turned into a lizard, but also that he performed a dozen or so other feats of an equally bizarre and 'impossible' nature, in each case the event occurring only after he had called upon his god Mazda to show his power.

single event, even if verified, can be a statistical fluke or a one-off anomaly. But a *pattern* changes everything. This is the principle of **convergence of evidence**.
*   **Event 1:** Pencil to lizard. (Could be a trick.)
*   **Event 2:** Water to wine. (Could be a different trick.)
*   **Event 12:** A stone to float. (Could be a third trick.)

If all these events share a common feature—specifically, that they *only* happen when the prophet calls upon Mazda—the probability that they are all independent, unrelated natural phenomena or separate tricks drops to near zero. The common cause becomes the most parsimonious explanation. The "invisible agent" hypothesis starts to look like the best fit for the data.

Finally, lest there still remain any stiff-necked sceptics in his audience, our prophet invites members of the crowd of witnesses to name a half-a-dozen or more equally impossible events which he will ask Mazda to cause to come to pass at various specified intervals after the prophet's own death, and behold these events all do subsequently happen, and at precisely the times predicted.⁹

is the "nail in the coffin" for the skeptic. This step introduces **post-mortem prediction**.
1.  **Removal of the Agent:** The prophet dies. This eliminates the possibility that he is the one performing the magic tricks. He cannot be hiding wires or chemicals if he is deceased.
2.  **Specificity:** The events are named by the *audience*, not the prophet. This prevents the prophet from preparing for specific tricks.
3.  **Temporal Precision:** The events happen at *precisely* the predicted times.

If a dead man’s predictions come true with perfect accuracy, and the events are physically impossible by natural standards, the only remaining explanatory framework is that the prophet was indeed communicating with an entity capable of overriding natural laws. The "invisible agent" is no longer a hypothesis; it is the only logical conclusion left standing after all naturalistic alternatives have been exhausted.

is the crux of the argument. The author is defending a specific type of reasoning known as **teleological explanation**. Teleology refers to explanations based on purpose, intent, or design, rather than just mechanical cause-and-effect. When we see a pattern of events that seems random or chaotic, but which actually points toward a specific goal or outcome, we often look for an "agent"—a being with intentions—behind it.

Consider a concrete example: You find a series of stones arranged in a perfect circle in the middle of a forest.
1.  **Mechanical Explanation:** Wind and erosion randomly moved the stones. (Highly improbable, requires many "coincidences").
2.  **Teleological Explanation:** A person placed them there intentionally. (Simple, economical, explains the pattern).

The trick (the "violation" of our expectations) is only possible because the rest of the stage, the lighting, and the physics of the audience’s perception remain normal. 2.  Within this stable baseline, we observe a specific, localized anomaly (a "violation" of specific physical or biological laws).

The agent’s actions "unify" the events. Without the agent, the events are disjointed, random, and inexplicable. With the agent, they become a coherent story.

When any miracle story is presented to us, if we are reasonable we surely must, as Hume insists, consider whether it is more probable that the report of the event is due to human error, self-deception, fraud and the like than due to its actually having happened. Which of each pair of these alternatives is the more probable with regard to the miracle stories contained in the extant literature of the great world religions seems to me to be beyond reasonable doubt.

At this point it is relevant to return to the remarks I attributed to my Christian friend at the beginning of this paper. For it will no doubt be objected that what is considered probable with regard to miracles will very much depend on whether one already has a belief in an almighty personal god. Given such a belief, the probability of any miracle story's being true will depend not merely on the amount and quality of the relevant evidence, but also (and just as importantly) on whether the alleged miracle was of such a nature as could be fittingly attributed to the kind of god believed in. The probability of any particular miracle story (it will be said) is bound to be assessed very differently by one who already believes in an almighty, personal god than by someone who rejects such a belief. And such a discrepancy between the assessment of probabilities would seem only reasonable.

Except for one difficulty. How we could have any grounds at all for this prior belief in a personal god apart from evidence provided by a series of miracles is not easy to see. For it is surely part of the very concept of a personal being that such a being perform actions, at least from time to time. There could be no reason for attributing personal qualities to a being who literally never does anything, and never has done anything at all. It might be claimed that the very existence of an ordered universe is evidence for the existence of a supremely intelligent, personal being who designed it. Certainly if some version of the design argument could be shown to be sound, then conceivably this might provide us with some sort of foundational belief in a personal god which would make the occurrence of miracles initially more probable. Unfortunately the design argument is pretty widely agreed to be fallacious, justifiably in my view. In particular, those who appeal to a religious revelation are usually as convinced as anyone that neither the design argument nor any other traditional buttress of a natural theology can provide us with grounds for a belief in a personal god. And yet, assuming all versions of the design argument to be unsound, the only grounds we could have for belief in the existence of a personal god would be the occurrence of a fair number of well-attested miracles.
My Christian friend, therefore, was right to take the question of miracles seriously. Perhaps his mistake was in not taking it seriously enough.
